steps.explanationAfterStep: The allylic cation is delocalised: the positive charge is shared between the carbon that lost chlorine and the end CH₂ carbon. Both can be attacked.
Attack at the secondary carbon leads to but-3-en-2-ol. That carbon is the more substituted end and carries more of the positive charge.
Also correct: attack at the end CH₂ carbon, with the double bond moving over. This leads to but-2-en-1-ol, the other regioisomer, which also forms. An allylic cation gives a mixture.
But-3-en-2-ol: water has replaced chlorine on the same carbon.
But-2-en-1-ol: the OH is on the end carbon and the double bond has moved one position along the chain.

title: Hydrolysis of an allylic chloride
subtitle: One cation, two ends, two alcohols
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 15

reactants.caption: 3-chlorobut-1-ene + water
hintTiers: Breaking the C–Cl bond would put the positive charge next to a C=C double bond. Why is that a good place for it?
The C–Cl bond breaks on its own, both electrons going to chlorine. One arrow.
The C–Cl bond breaks, and its pair goes onto chlorine, leaving an allylic cation.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Show the first step in water.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Water is a weak nucleophile. Here the C–Cl bond ionises first, because the cation it gives is allylic and stabilised by the C=C bond.
The C–Cl pair goes to chlorine, the more electronegative atom.

end-products.caption: but-2-en-1-ol (the other regioisomer, also formed) + hydronium chloride

allylic-cation.caption: the allylic cation (one resonance form drawn)
hintTiers: Picture the other resonance form: the charge is shared by the inner, secondary carbon and the end CH₂ carbon. Which carries more of it?
Water attacks the secondary carbon, the one chlorine left, which carries more of the positive charge. One arrow.
The lone pair on water's oxygen forms a new bond to the positive secondary carbon.
allylic-cation.learnerPrompt: Water can attack either end of the allylic cation. Draw the attack that gives the main product.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That re-forms the starting chloride. Water is in huge excess and traps the cation as the alcohol.
Chloride can add at the end carbon too, giving 1-chlorobut-2-ene: this allylic rearrangement does happen. But water is in huge excess, and it traps the cation as the alcohol.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: That moves the charge to the end carbon: the other resonance form. Attack there is possible too (it gives the other alcohol), but draw the water arrow in the same step.

primary-oxonium-ion.caption: protonated but-2-en-1-ol
hintTiers: The O–H bond of a positively charged oxygen is acidic. Which molecule present can act as a base?
A second water takes the proton from the positive oxygen; the O–H pair stays on that oxygen. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: a lone pair of a second water forms a bond to the hydrogen on the positive oxygen. Arrow 2: that O–H bond breaks, and its pair goes back onto the oxygen.
primary-oxonium-ion.learnerPrompt: Remove the proton to give the alcohol.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Chloride is a very weak base (HCl is a strong acid). Water, the solvent, takes the proton.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right base, right proton. Hydrogen can only have one bond: where does the old O–H pair go?

mechanismSummary: SN1 through an allylic cation. The positive charge is shared by two carbons, so water attacks both: at the carbon chlorine left, giving but-3-en-2-ol, and at the far end, with the double bond moving along, giving but-2-en-1-ol. 1-Chlorobut-2-ene ionises to the same cation and gives the same two alcohols.
